title: Garter stitch triangle shawl
subtitle: A top-down triangle in plain garter stitch, worked flat.
excerpt: A top-down triangular shawl worked entirely in garter stitch, cast on at the centre back neck and increased every right-side row to a wingspan of 145 cm. No lace, no charts, no special techniques: knit every row and let the stitch do the work. About 350 g of DK wool.
sourceNotes: Elizabeth Zimmermann, Knitting Without Tears (1971), §The Pi Shawl family. The top-down triangle with a garter-tab cast-on and four-stitch-per-RS-row increase is the core of EZ's shawl vocabulary and appears in all major twentieth-century hand-knitting reference works. Weldon's Practical Knitter, 2nd series (1886), §Shawls, uses the same three-needle start.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small strip of garter stitch worked on a few stitches, then rotated so live stitches can be picked up from all three edges, giving a neat triangular start at the centre back neck.
Wrapping the yarn over the right needle before knitting the next stitch. Leaves a small eyelet hole and adds one stitch to the count.

content.text: A top-down triangular shawl in DK wool, worked flat in garter stitch from a three-stitch centre-back start to a wingspan of 145 cm and a centre-back depth of 68 cm.

The construction runs top-down: you start at the centre back neck with three stitches, then increase four stitches on every right-side row until the wingspan reaches the length you want. Top-down lets you try the shawl across your shoulders as it grows, so you can stop at exactly the right depth without committing to a stitch count in advance. Every row is a knit row, so there is nothing to track except the increases. Budget about 350 g (about 770 m / 840 yards) of DK wool. This drapes across the shoulders held at the centre back, or wraps around the neck as a large cowl.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 350 g (770 m / 840 yards) of DK-weight yarn
items.substitutions: Any DK wool or wool blend. A 100% wool or 80% wool blend gives the best drape and blocks well. Acrylic will not block to the same dimensions.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) single straight or circular needle, 80 cm or longer

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 3 — one at each increase point and one at the centre back spine

items.name: Waste yarn
items.qty: About 30 cm for the provisional cast-on

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. Take a 15 cm square swatch, wash and block it flat, let it dry, then measure the centre 10 cm. Garter stitch pulls in slightly when unblocked and opens by about 8% after blocking, so the unblocked swatch will read a little tighter than the blocked number.

If your blocked gauge is 23 stitches per 10 cm instead of 22, the finished wingspan will be about 138 cm rather than 145 cm at the same row count. If your gauge is 21 stitches per 10 cm, the wingspan will reach about 152 cm. Move up or down one needle size to bring your gauge in line before starting.
Stitches used

items.name: yo
items.qty: yarn over: bring the yarn to the front, then over the needle before the next stitch. Adds one stitch and leaves a small eyelet.

content.text: Pattern
Garter tab cast-on
The shawl starts with a
garter tab
that anchors the centre back point cleanly.
Using waste yarn and a knitted-on cast-on, cast on 3 stitches.
Knit 6 rows in garter stitch with the waste yarn. You now have a small rectangle with 3 loops live on the needle, 3 loops visible along one long edge, and the cast-on edge at the bottom.
Switch to the main yarn. Knit the 3 live stitches on the needle (RS row).
Without turning, rotate the rectangle 90 degrees and pick up and knit 3 stitches along the long left-hand edge of the tab (one stitch per garter ridge). That is 6 stitches total on the needle.
Without turning again, pick up and knit 3 stitches along the cast-on edge (unpick the waste yarn as you go). Total: 9 stitches.

Knit 1 WS row across all 9 stitches. Place markers: marker A after st 1, marker B (spine) after st 5, marker C after st 8. The shawl sits: 1 edge st, 3 left-wing sts, 1 spine st, 3 right-wing sts, 1 edge st.
Increase section
Work the two-row repeat until the wingspan reaches 145 cm. Each RS row adds 4 stitches (one
yarn over increase
before and after each marker, four markers total). Every WS row is a plain knit row.
RS row (increase row): k1, yo, SM, k to 1 st before marker B, yo, k1, SM, k1, yo, SM, k to last 1 st, yo, k1. (4 sts increased, RS row)
WS row: k across all sts. (WS)
Repeat these two rows. After 40 RS rows you will have 9 + (4 × 40) = 169 stitches. After 80 RS rows: 329 stitches. After 170 RS rows (when the wingspan reaches 145 cm at gauge): 689 stitches.
Stitch count check-ins
After 40 RS rows (about 25 cm from the centre back neck): you should have 169 stitches. A count of 165 or 173 means one or two increase rows were missed or doubled.
After 100 RS rows (about 62 cm from the centre back neck): you should have 409 stitches. This is a good midpoint check before the remaining rows consume a second skein.
Bind off

Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off: *k1, yarn over to the front, k1, pass the yarn-over and first knit stitch over the second knit stitch together; repeat from *. This bind-off is deliberately longer to work than a standard bind-off. A standard bind-off on a garter shawl holds the edge taut and fights blocking, leaving the wingspan 10 to 15 cm shorter than the pinned dimensions after the pins come out.
Common faults

Yarn overs worked on the wrong side of the marker: the eyelet appears in the body instead of at the spine edge. Check that every yo is placed one stitch before or immediately after the marker, not two stitches away.

Tight bind-off that fights the pin: a standard bind-off here pulls the top edge tight and the wingspan springs back after unpinning. Jeny's stretchy bind-off is specified for this reason. Work it loose and even.

Stitch count drifting every few rows: a marker was knocked off the needle and the next row's increase was worked one stitch away from the spine. Count stitches every 20 RS rows and reposition the markers if the two wings go out of balance.
Blocking

Soak the finished shawl in cool water with a wool wash for 15 minutes. Lift it out without wringing and press firmly in towels to remove most of the water. Lay flat on a blocking mat. Pin the centre back neck point at the top, then pin the two lower corner points out to a wingspan of 145 cm and a centre-back depth of 68 cm. Use about 20 to 30 pins along the two sloped edges to keep the triangle flat and the edge straight. Leave to dry completely, which takes about 24 hours in a warm room.
Care

Hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent, or machine wash on a delicate cycle at 30 degrees if the yarn label allows. Lay flat to dry. Do not wring or tumble dry. Re-block on the pins if the shape softens after several washes.
What to try next

The natural next step is a lace triangle. The construction is the same: same garter tab, same four-stitch increase every RS row, same top-down shape. The only change is adding a feather-and-fan or eyelet repeat in the body rows between increases.
